objectives: Through readings, videos, lectures, and class assignments, students will learn key concepts of news media, including the relationship between journalism and society.
Students will learn about the First Amendment, including their rights.
Students will become more critical consumers of media via a focus on current media controversies and events.
Students will be introduced to media history, ethics, and law.
topics: Reading and using news; building blocks of news; media
processes and principles; the structure and nature of media;
watching TV news: how to be a smarter viewer; anatomy of a
multimedia news organization; how news is made; history of
journalism in America; theories of the First Amendment;
freedom of information; newsgathering law and liability;
freedom of the press; online media law: basics for bloggers
and others; handling race and ethnicity; journalism ethics;
politics and media; understanding and interpreting polls;
media as a business; hate speech and campus speech codes;
free-speech zones; fan profanity; sexual harassment.

Students will be able to interrogate typography, color, and visuals based on the principles of design for context, news delivery, and readability purposes.
Students will be able to craft digital design elements using various tools and programs with iterative processes.

Students will assess, through critical conversations with peers and the professor, how well the U.S. media covers faith and religion.
Students will demonstrate appropriate interviewing techniques with faith leaders, religion researchers, and active members of religious groups at UGA and in the Athens area.
Students will navigate the complexities of writing about religion across platforms.
Students will author high-quality faith reporting that avoids bias, aligns to journalistic standards and style, and uses modes of media required in today’s media world.

objectives: Students will analyze and critique visual messages using multiple theoretical frameworks to understand how meaning is constructed through media images.
Students will understand how we physically, and socially "see," incorporating theories of visual perception and communication to interpret news imagery.

Students will critically evaluate how visual news media represent people, events, and cultures, with emphasis on ethical responsibility, cultural awareness, and the power dynamics embedded in visual storytelling.
